newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Skoda seen boosting VW globalisation effort.
newsitem.headline: Skoda seen boosting VW globalisation effort.

text.p: Czech automaker Skoda automobilova AS will play a growing role in the globalisation efforts of its majority owner Volkswagen AG now that it has returned to profitability, analysts said on Thursday.
Skoda, owned 70 percent by VW, reported its first profit under international accounting standards on Thursday, posting earnings of 163 million crowns ($5.7 million).

The results follow losses of 1.6 billion crowns in 1995, 2.4 billion crowns in 1994 and 4.3 billion crowns in 1993. Skoda reported a profit of 4.2 billion crowns in 1992 under old Czech accounting standards.
"This makes a big difference for VW's strategy in growth markets around the world," Jim Gillette, vice president at U.S. automotive consultancy International Resource Network Inc, told Reuters.
"VW invested a lot of money and technology in Skoda to achieve ecOnomies of scale with the aim of generating greater profits per vehicle, and that investment is starting to pay off."

The German automaker has invested 1.4 billion marks in the Czech automaker since buying a minority stake in 1991. Skoda also has invested 1.8 billion marks to expand and modernise its operations in the past seven years.
Skoda, the oldest car brand in central and eastern Europe, is the region's first automaker to shed its communist-era model range while preserving its identity.

Other automakers have survived only by forming joint ventures with foreign investors, resulting in discontinuation of their model range. Romania's Oltcit stopped producing its cars shortly after creating a company called Automobile Rodae SA with South Korea's Daewoo Group.

VW -- which also owns SEAT and luxury-brand Audi -- has brought Skoda closely into its family of vehicles by sharing major components such as chassis and engines, not immediately visible to consumers.

This cooperation also will enable VW to start introducing production of Skoda models at plants where the German automaker already assembles cars, especially in Latin America and Southeast Asia, analysts said.

"VW has an experimental plant in Brazil with a limited number of company employees because a lot of the components are outsourced to systems suppliers," Gillette said. "It would not be hard for VW to modify operations there to build Skodas."
Skoda itself has been studying car production opportunities in other developing markets, such as Egypt and India.
The Czech automaker already has played a key role in VW's efforts to develop a presence in the old East bloc.
Skoda accounts for over half of all vehicles that VW sells in the region. It assembles cars in Poland, and assembly operations are planned for Belarus and Russia.
Analysts also expect Skoda to play a greater role for VW in western Europe.

"VW seems quite determined to take the VW brand upwards to compete with Mercedes-Benz, and that leaves quite a lot of room for Skoda to market itself as the value brand in western Europe," Philip Wade, a partner in British automotive consultancy Harbour Wade Brown, told Reuters.
